items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-19
items.q: his name appears with Barney Begard's on Mood Indigo

ctx.x: Or that his name appears with Barney Begard's on Mood Indigo, which Barney Begard had nothing to do with the composition of that either. Take the A train, says Hodges Ellington. This is all true. But what I'm saying is that in none of these cases did Ellington make any contribution to the composition. These were all compositions of these various people. Now, because of slick publicity, he has been presented as a great creative genius who has composed all these pieces.
But it's not just slick publicity, Al. It's people like Gunther Schuller who in their book, Early Jazz, call him the first great composer.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1989-08-13
items.q: he told me, Jack Teagarden, Barney Begard, and Sidney Catlett. And, the only one I didn't know was Arwell Shaw

ctx.x: And it was a black theater and I used to come out of, out of class and go across the street to the theater all the time, because I knew a lot of the musicians that were, that were playing in the, in the show. And it was during the time when I had first started doing jazz concerts. So it was 1936 and I went backstage, because his band was playing there. And I knew Louis Russell and Red Allen and people that were playing there, Al Nicholas. So, I had, I had met Louis before, I don't actually remember when, but…
Okay, we're on the second reel. Al Rose, same date. August 13th, 1989. Okay, we left off with Eus... Eus Panassia.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: his name appears with Barney Begard's on Mood Indigo, which Barney Begard had nothing to do with the composition of that either.

ctx.x: But isn't, Al, let me ask you this, isn't that the definition of a jazz composer to a certain extent, that he does draw upon his musicians in a way?

Well, it's not a question of drawing upon his musicians. It's the fact that he has literally used their material, you see, and the music is published with their names on it. It is not as though Ellington removed their identification. No, I mean, the point is that it says, sophisticated lady, Otto Hardwick and Duke Ellington. Unfortunately, I mean, it's not unethical for Ellington to have his name on it. That's not what I'm suggesting. Okay. Or that his name appears with Barney Begard's on Mood Indigo, which…
It's people like Gunther Schuller, who in their book, Early Jazz, call him the first great composer.
